A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_ Cellulose Hydrogels Adsorption

Wastewater treatment

A B S T R A C T

Cellulose-based hydrogels are versatile and biodegradable materials derived from renewable cellulose sources. These hydrogels possess unique properties, such as high water absorption capacity, tunable mechanical strength and excellent biocompatibility. Their porous structure and functional groups enable effective interactions with contaminants and making them ideal candidates for water purification. In wastewater treatment, cellulose-based hydrogels are widely utilized for adsorbing heavy metals and dyes because of their exceptional adsorption ca-pacity and reusability. Chemical changes and enhanced fabrication processes can improve these materials ca-pacity to combat different contaminants under demanding environmental conditions. This review comprehensively explores the extraction and modification of cellulose, the functional and structural properties of cellulose derivatives and the synthesis techniques for cellulose-based hydrogels. It delves into the adsorption mechanisms and highlighting their efficiency in removing specific contaminants. Factors influencing adsorption behavior, such as crosslink density, pollutant concentration, pH, temperature and ionic strength are also dis-cussed. Finally, review outlines current challenges and provides future perspectives to guide research and innovation in this field. It emphasizes the potential of cellulose-based hydrogels as sustainable solutions for wastewater remediation.

# Introduction

Every living thing on Earth depends on water. While it covers most of the planet but only 3 % is freshwater and with an even smaller portion usable by humans. This scarcity underscores the necessity of recycling and prudent water management. With the global population surpassing 8 billion in 2023, freshwater demand is rising. Climate change exacer-bates the problem by altering rainfall patterns, which results in short-ages. Industrial activities like textile production and oil refining pollute water by releasing harmful substances, reducing clean water availability and harming ecosystems \[[1](#_bookmark20)\]. As industrialization grows, access to safe drinking water becomes costlier and challenging. By 2025, two-thirds of

global population may face water scarcity, endangering ecosystems and human health \[[2](#_bookmark21)\].

To address these challenges, conserving water, improving recycling and adopting sustainable practices are vital. Pollutants like heavy metals and dyes can be treated through filtration, photochemical methods and adsorption, categorized into chemical, physical or biological processes. Hydrogels are emerging as an effective wastewater treatment solution due to their water absorption, customizable structure and pollutant removal efficiency \[[3](#_bookmark22)\]. Hydrogels are a type of polymeric compound containing hydrophilic polymer chains and a 3D network structure. They absorb water because of the hydrophilic groups found in their polymer network. The functional groups like OH, SO3H, COOH, NH2,

and CONH2 are responsible for the swelling, cross-linked bonding and the water-absorbable capacity phenomenon in hydrogels. Hydrogels use physical or chemical linking to preserve their structure throughout swelling process. Temporary connections are created through electro-static, hydrophobic, or hydrogen bonding interactions during physical cross-linking \[[4](#_bookmark23),[5](#_bookmark24)\]. On the contrary, chemical crosslinking creates du-rable connections through the increased ionic communication and co-valent bonding. During polymerization, several polymeric structures, i. e., homo-polymers, graft _co_\-polymers and linear co-polymers, are created through physical/chemical crosslinking. There are various types of hydrogels being utilized in research areas, including solid molded form (for soft contact lens), micro-particles (for wound treatment), pressed powders matrices (for oral ingestion of pills/capsules), coating (for materials protection), and liquid (which turns to gel by heating or cooling). Hydrogels can be created chemically or derived from natural sources (natural hydrogels). Natural hydrogels, often referred to as hydrogels made of biopolymers and they have special qualities like biocompatibility and non-toxicity \[[6](#_bookmark25)\]. The most popular natural biopolymer is cellulose. It is very desirable because it is safe to produce and it is also non-toxic. There is a growing need for these products in many different kinds of applications. Cellulose is present in plant cell walls and it is found in most commonly extracted from cotton and wood. Plant cellulose is also known as lignocellulose and it is a composite material that joins hemicellulose with lignin to form a composite structure. Cellulose acts as a stiff polymer that provides strength and structure within plants. Chemically speaking, cellulose is formed of chains of pyranose anhydrous glucose that are linear and unbranched. At the C1 and C4 places, ether linkage connects these units together. The amazing properties of cellulose are a result of this unusual molecular structure ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark10)) \[[7](#_bookmark26),[8](#_bookmark27)\].

For cellulose the degree of polymerization varies, ranging from 500

to 15,000 and it depending on sources and the methods used for its chemical and physical treatment. Cellulose is normally hydrophobic and not susceptible to hydrolysis in its unaltered form. However, cellulose molecules are capable of decomposition by acidic or enzymatic (cellu-lase) hydrolysis and leading to a noticeably smaller and lighter molec-ular structure. The hydroxyl groups in cellulose form hydrogen bonds with other hydroxyl groups nearby and which promotes crystallization and gives cellulose its semi-crystalline structure \[[9](#_bookmark28)\]. Pure cellulose nanocrystal is fabricated by hydrolysis of acid, which selectively hy-drolyzes the amorphous areas. Numerous industrial uses for these cel-lulose nanocrystals exist, such as the reinforcement of fillers in composite manufacture. Similarly, bacterial cellulose occurs naturally and can be made by bacteria (i.e., Acetobacter xylinum). Both glucose and sucrose are essential carbon sources but glucose provides larger amounts of bacterial cellulose than sucrose. Plant and bacterial cellulose have the same chemical structure, but they differ greatly in terms of their physicochemical properties and polymerization degrees \[[10](#_bookmark29)\]. Both of these materials have found use in several sectors, including the biomedical, pharmaceutical, food, textile and paper industries, because of their distinct molecular structure and special physicochemical qual-ities. The structured crystalline regions of cellulose must break down in order to promote its dissolution through modification techniques. This is because hydroxyl groups have many hydrogen bonds with one another. A variety of cellulose ethers, often referred to as cellulose derivative, are created by etherifying the hydroxyl group in cellulose. Additionally, the increased surface area and higher concentration of hydroxyl groups in

Researchers utilize the adsorptive properties of the cellulose for water remediation applications \[[11](#_bookmark30)\]. The hydrogel made from the cellulose are biocompatible and biodegradable as opposed to conventionally prepared hydrogels. Most of the conventionally available hydrogels are made from petrochemicals making them unsuitable for reuse. Using cellulose based hydrogel in place of petrochemical hydrogels could help in making the adsorption a more viable approach for removing the pollutants from the water. Literature shows the potential of utilizing cellulose based hydrogel for the water remediation. Zhou et al. suc-cessfully utilized carboxylate cellulose hydrogel for adsorption of various heavy metals. Removal efficiencies of about 90 % (in 4 h) was achieved for Pb(II) with adsorption tendency of 171 mg/g \[[12](#_bookmark31)\]. Yang et al. showed adsorptive potential of cellulose hydrogel towards adsorption of Ni(II) and Cu(II) was realized. Their study showed good adsorption behavior of cellulose based hydrogel for Cu(II) and Ni(II) attaining adsorption of 182 and 200 mg/g respectively \[[13](#_bookmark32)\]. These studies show that the cellulose based hydrogel is efficient in removing numerous types of metallic ions form the water. Some studies have also demonstrated the usefulness of this material for removing the dyes. Jung et al. showed dye adsorption process via the cellulose based hydrogel. Their prepared material showed adsorption 372 and 140.5 mg/g to-wards the acid orange and methylene blue dyes. The samples also showed good reusability and retained about 95 % of its adsorptive na-ture even after 5 reuses \[[14](#_bookmark33)\]. These studies demonstrate that using the cellulose based hydrogel is viable for eliminating organic and inorganic pollutants for the aqueous system.

This review focuses on our innovative contributions to knowledge of

cellulose-based hydrogels for water remediation. Unlike existing litera-ture, this study provides a thorough examination of the connection be-tween the structural and functional features of cellulose derivatives and their adsorptive tendencies. We highlight the importance of water sol-ubility, tunability, biocompatibility, and biodegradability in deter-mining their efficacy, with an emphasis on how chemical modifications improve these characteristics. Our comprehensive approach stands out by investigating a broad range of cellulose derivatives, identifying their distinct structural characteristics and analyzing their impact on adsorption processes. Our study, which addresses key challenges in wastewater treatment, highlights revolutionary capacity of cellulose-based hydrogels in offering sustainable and effective solutions. Furthermore, we identify developing trends and highlight unexplored prospects in this sector, providing a forward-looking view of the future of cellulose-based hydrogels. In order to promote innovation and propel breakthroughs in biomaterial-based water remediation solutions, the review acts as a call to action for researchers to further explore this exciting field.

# Cellulose extraction

Cellulose is a carbohydrate polymer that serves as a vital structural component in plants. It was first discovered by the French chemist Anselme Payen in 1838. Payen used ether, alcohol, and water to extract various plant tissues after treating them with acid and ammonia in his research \[[15](#_bookmark34)\]. Through this process, he identified a fibrous solid that remained resistant to these treatments. Payen performed an elemental analysis and determined the molecular formula of cellulose to be C6H10O5. He also observed that cellulose is an isomer of starch. The term “cellulose” was officially introduced in 1839 in a report by the French Academy based on Payen’s pioneering work \[[16](#_bookmark35)\].

Cellulose, as a vital structural polymer in plants, has significant ap-plications due to its abundance and versatility. It is extracted from various sources, including lignocellulosic biomass such as jute, hemp, rice husk, and banana fibers. The growing demand for environmentally friendly materials has also encouraged the utilization of agricultural waste for cellulose extraction, offering a sustainable approach to waste

management and material production \[[16](#_bookmark35)\]. Agricultural residues like coconut hulls, coffee husk, wheat straw, banana rachis, and peanut shells are commonly used for this purpose, as depicted in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark11).

The extraction of cellulose fibers can produce nano or micro-sized forms, depending on the method employed. Various chemical and me-chanical processes are available for isolating cellulose from these sour-ces. The extraction typically involves three main steps: pre-hydrolysis, pulping, and bleaching \[[17](#_bookmark36)\].

- **Pre-hydrolysis**: In this initial step, alkali or mineral acids are used to disrupt the lignin and hemicellulose matrix, preparing the material for further processing.
- **Pulping**: The material is heated with alkali, such as sodium hy-

droxide (NaOH), to separate the cellulose fibers from other components.

- **Bleaching**: This final step enhances the purity of the cellulose.

Various chemicals, such as hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), sulfuric acid (H2SO4), ozone, and sodium chlorite, are used under specific con-ditions to achieve high-quality bleached cellulose.

Agricultural waste represents a promising resource for cellulose extraction, addressing both material demand and waste disposal issues. In underdeveloped nations, where agricultural residues often become an environmental burden, the conversion of waste into valuable cellulose is an especially significant solution \[[16](#_bookmark35)\]. For instance, banana peels, ba-nana rachis, and rice husks are effective sources for cellulose extraction, aligning with the global trend towards sustainable biopolymer devel-opment \[[18](#_bookmark37)\].

The cellulose extracted from such sources is utilized in diverse uses, ranging from textiles and packaging to advanced fields like nanotech-nology and biomedicine. This approach not only reduces waste but also

supports the development of eco-friendly materials, making cellulose extraction from agricultural residues a key area of study for sustainable innovation.

# Cellulose derivatives

Cellulose is made more useful and versatile through chemical treat-ments and functionalization. These processes create cellulose de-rivatives that are broadly utilized in biomedical field. The qualities of these derivatives based on two key factors: type and amount of chemical changes made to the cellulose and how these changes are arranged along the cellulose chain \[[19](#_bookmark38)\]. Like the etherification process is essential in production of cellulose-based derivatives. Etherification occurs when cellulose’s active hydroxyl groups chemically combine with organic substances like ethyl units and resulting in the production of additional functional groups. This reaction changes the chemical structure of cel-lulose and making the resultant water-soluble derivative \[[20](#_bookmark39)\]. During etherification, the hydroxyl groups on cellulose act as nucleophiles and initiating the reaction with the organic compound. In the case of ethyl units, the hydroxyl group of cellulose reacts with ethyl halide, typically ethyl chloride or ethyl bromide. This reaction results in the replacement of an ethyl for the hydrogen atom of hydroxyl group and leading in production of an ether bond \[[21](#_bookmark40)\]. The replacement of hydroxyl group in cellulose with ethyl units results in formation of ethyl cellulose. The existence of ethyl groups disturbs the vast bonding network, lowering intermolecular forces and enhancing derivative’s solubility in solvents. The degree of substitution is an important characteristic that controls the extent of etherification and cellulose derivative solubility. It is the mean amount of hydroxyl groups substituted in cellulose by ethyl units per glucose unit. Higher degree of substitution values imply that the derivative has a higher degree of substitution and is more water soluble.

**Fig. 2.** Name of some agricultural waste materials for the extraction of cellulose.

Water-soluble cellulose derivatives produced via etherification provide significant advantages in a variety of applications. These derivatives possess improved process ability and allowing them to be easily dis-solved and formulated into solutions, gels or films \[[22](#_bookmark41)\]. Because of their solubility, they can be utilized in biological usages like drug delivery and wound dressings. Ethyl cellulose, have special features that make them useful materials in the pharmaceutical business. They can be employed to manage medication release as film coatings for tablets or as viscosity modifiers in liquid formulations. Furthermore, the flexibility to change the degree of substitution allows for exact tailoring of the cellulose de-rivatives’ characteristics to meet specific application needs \[[9](#_bookmark28)\]. Ac-cording to Marques-Marinho et al. water-soluble cellulose derivatives encompass various compounds like methylcellulose, hydroxyethyl methylcellulose, ethyl cellulose, and hydroxypropyl cellulose \[[23](#_bookmark42)\]. The substitution is carefully controlled to attain the desired solubility of these cellulose derivatives in water-based solutions. Due to their distinct functional characteristics, ester derivatives of cellulose are utilized different types of industries. These polymers are created here by ester-ifying cellulosic hydroxyl with different organic acids while using a strong acid as a catalyst \[[24](#_bookmark43)\].

- 1.  _Structural properties of cellulose derivatives_

![](data:image/png;base64,)Cellulose molecules consist of glucose units and each possessing three unoccupied hydroxyl groups capable of forming robust intra-molecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds. This characteristic is clearly observed when examining the chemical composition of cellulose. These hydrogen bonds give cellulose its rigidity, crystalline structure and make it almost completely insoluble in numerous solvents, including water \[[25](#_bookmark44)\]. Ionic liquids are known as solvents that are favorable to the environment and are frequently used by researchers to dissolve cellulose in a variety of solvent systems. These ionic liquid systems include NaOH/urea and NaOH/thiourea, for examples. How-ever, there are certain drawbacks for using them, including high energy intake, high costs and challenges in solvent recovery. Controlled chemical or physical surface changes are crucial in enhancing the sol-ubility of cellulose and expanding its range of potential applications. Various cellulose derivatives can be created by disorganizing the orderly crystalline areas that are held with multiple hydrogen bonds in hydroxyl groups of cellulose \[[7](#_bookmark26)\]. [Fig. 3](#_bookmark12) depicts the two main processes used to create cellulose derivatives are etherification and esterification. In terms of distinctive properties of these derivates are chemical composition, hygroscopicity, interaction with water, surface activity and solubility. A

wider range of uses and customized features are made possible by the transformation of cellulose into derivatives \[[26](#_bookmark45)\].

Reagents, like alkyl halides, can partially or completely etherify cellulose. Cellulose derivatives are generally water-soluble, and cellu-lose ethers’ water solubility is dependent on substituent’s chemical structure. The cellulose ether derivatives have several advantageous qualities, including high stability against oxidative, thermal, and bio-logical degradation, solubility, solution viscosity, and surface activity \[[27](#_bookmark46)\]. Additionally, it is thought that cellulose ethers’ hydrophilicity, thermogelling ability and pH stability promote wound healing. [Fig. 4](#_bookmark13) illustrates the structural formulas of the four cellulose ethers \[[7](#_bookmark26)\].

With traits including water solubility, non-toxicity, biocompatible nature, and biodegradability, carboxymethyl cellulose is a commer-cialised form of cellulose ether, it is among the least expensive polymers. The hydroxyl group on C2, C3, and C6 of glucose residue are changed to carboxymethyl groups during cellulose and monochloroacetic acid re-action to create carboxymethyl cellulose. In biomedicine, 0.6 to 1.25 is often the ideal degree of carboxymethyl cellulose replacement. The location of carboxymethyl in polymer chain also has an impact on the characteristics of carboxymethyl cellulose. Sodium salt of carbox-ymethyl cellulose, is water-soluble and frequently utilized in wound dressings because it absorbs exudates and prevent tissue necrosis and skin tissues dryness \[[28](#_bookmark47)\].

![](data:image/png;base64,)The cellulose derivatives ethyl cellulose and methyl cellulose are used extensively throughout numerous industries. These derivatives have comparable chemical compositions. Alkali cellulose and ethyl chloride combine to create ethyl cellulose, which may be identified by its relative molecular mass, viscous nature and level of substitutions \[[29](#_bookmark48)\]. However, ethyl cellulose becomes extremely intractable when the degree of substitution increases. At room temperature, ethyl cellulose has good strength, but as the temperature rises, its strength rapidly declines. Additionally, ethyl cellulose offers low toxicity, thermoplas-ticity, hydrophobicity, and biodegradability. It is a superb material for a variety of industries due to its exceptional film-forming capacity and suitable mechanical attributes \[[30](#_bookmark49)\]. Methyl cellulose, on the other hand, is created when cellulose etherify with methyl chloride sulphate in an alkaline medium. Based on the level of substitutions, methyl cellulose has low crystallinity and is soluble in various organic solvents. Notably, in aqueous solutions, methyl cellulose exhibits reversible sol-gel tran-sition thermosensitive behavior with temperature fluctuations. Methyl cellulose is frequently used in biomedical industries due to its strong biocompatible as well as biodegradability nature \[[31](#_bookmark50)\]. Hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose is manufactured by when hydroxyl replaces methyl and hydroxypropyl group, which ultimately yields a powder with a white colour and a fibrous or granular texture. This cellulose derivative finds wide application in control release formulations due to its ability to swell, thicken, gel and respond to temperature changes. In the waste water remediation, hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose shows good

potential due to its desirable traits, including low toxicity, biocompat-ible nature, biodegradability, high stability and excellent surface ac-tivity \[[32](#_bookmark51)\].

Acetic, nitric and phosphoric acids can be used to esterify cellulose to create water-insoluble ester. It exhibits favorable solubility in typical solvent and undergo melting before undergoing decomposition. In general, two kinds of cellulose esters are: organic and inorganic, with the former being more commonly used in the biomedical industry. Cellulose acetate can be made using ring-opening esterification, trans-

Additionally, current cellulose acetate preparation methods do not call for additional mechanical or chemical cellulose processing, which is advantageous for tissue engineering methods. Beneficial mechanical qualities, hydrophobicity, biocompatible, non-toxicity nature and lower cost are a few of cellulose acetates noteworthy properties that are linked to its natural origin. The degree of nitrification determines the kind and use of nitrocellulose, which is created when cellulose and nitric acid react \[[34](#_bookmark53)\]. Cellulose sulphate is a cellulose ester having simple chain formation and specific biological characteristics that can be synthesized using heterogeneous, quasi-homogeneous or homogeneous sulphate techniques. Evaluated with pure cellulose, cellulose sulphate has supe-rior qualities because of sulphate groups, including high amounts of water solubility, antimicrobial, and anticoagulant properties. It is beneficial for tissue engineering owing to simplicity of synthesis, lower cost, and high biocompatibility and biodegradability \[[35](#_bookmark54)\].

The structural characteristics of cellulose derivatives are profoundly influenced through their chemical composition and functional modifi-cations. The formation of cellulose derivatives, through processes like etherification and esterification, enhances their solubility, stability and versatility. Key derivatives like carboxymethyl cellulose, ethyl cellulose, methyl cellulose and cellulose acetate exhibit properties like biode-gradability, biocompatibility and mechanical strength. These attributes make them invaluable in fields like biomedical engineering, tissue scaffolding, and wastewater remediation. Moreover, these advance-ments underscore the potential of tailored cellulose derivatives to address industrial and environmental challenges effectively.

# Cellulose based hydrogel: structure and traits

Cellulose hydrogels are three-dimensional structures classified on the bases of crosslinking and configurations. Based on configurations these hydrogels can either be amorphous, crystalline or semi-crystalline. Based on crosslinking, there exists two possibilities i.e., either physical or chemical bonding. Furthermore, hydrogel composite could also be made, either as interpenetrating polymer network or as nanoparticles and hydrogel composites. Cellulose-based hydrogel exhibits distinct traits making them highly appealing for a variety of uses. Biodegrad-ability and swelling mechanisms are being the two most important properties. Studying biodegradability and swelling mechanisms is crit-ical for improving performance and adapting features to specific appli-cations. Researchers can accurately manage the biodegradation rate and swelling behavior by changing the crosslinking densities, modifying the hydrogel composition, or introducing functional groups \[[36](#_bookmark55)\]. This un-derstanding paves the way for the creation of innovative materials with tailored degradation profiles and responsive swelling properties boost-ing their usefulness and adaptability in a variety of sectors. Both of these traits are further explained for better understanding.

- 1.  _Swelling and mechanical traits_

Hydrogel swelling is a phenomenon of significant scientific interest that provides insights into its behavior and mechanisms responsible for maintaining 3D form of hydrogels in solvent systems. The swelling process depends on factors, like presence of dissociated sodium carboxylate groups and hydrophilic groups within the hydrogel matrix.

Which contribute to the osmotic pressure increase and subsequent swelling. Hydrogels containing dissociated sodium carboxylate groups and hydrophilic groups exhibit an enhanced swelling behavior. The

dissociation of carboxylate groups leads to the release of sodium ions (Na+) into the solvent and which increases the osmotic pressure \[[37](#_bookmark56)\]. This pressure gradient drives the absorption of solvent molecules and

causing the hydrogel to swell. The hydrophilic group also contributes to the hydrogel’s swelling behavior by facilitating water absorption due to their strong affinity for water molecules. The repulsive forces between negatively charged particles play a fundamental role in the swelling. As hydrogel absorbs solvent, the polymer coils within the network expand. In hydrogels containing dissociated sodium carboxylate groups, the carboxylate ions repel each other, causing increased intermolecular distance and expanded polymer coils. This electrostatic repulsion further facilitates the swelling and contributes to volumetric expansion of the hydrogel. Conversely, crosslinking within hydrogels plays a crucial role in preventing their dissolution in water or solvents. Cross-links are chemical bonds that connect polymer chains in hydrogel network. These crosslinks provide mechanical integrity and stability to the hydrogel. The presence of crosslinks restricts the chains mobility and preventing the dissolution of the hydrogel in solvent environments. This structural integrity allows the hydrogel to maintain its three-dimensional shape even when exposed to stimuli. Understanding the complex interplay between swelling and crosslinking is crucial for designing hydrogels with desired properties and behaviors. By manip-ulating the composition, crosslinking density, and polymer architecture, researchers can tailor the swelling behavior of hydrogels for specific uses like drug delivery ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark14)) \[[38](#_bookmark57)\].

The swelling property and swelling degree of hydrogels are influ-

enced by several variables, including network density, solvent type and the polymer-solvent interaction parameter. These factors help in deter-mining the extent of swelling and the overall behavior of hydrogels in different environments. Network density is an essential parameter that affects the swelling behaviors. It refers to the concentration of crosslinks within polymer network. Higher network density corresponds to a higher number of crosslinks and resulting in a more tightly inter-connected structure. Hydrogels with a high network density typically exhibit lower swelling capacity due to restricted mobility \[[36](#_bookmark55)\]. The close proximity of crosslinks hinders absorption of solvent molecules and limiting the swelling degree. The type of solvent in which the hydrogel is immersed also significantly impacts its swelling behavior. Solvents can be good solvents and poor solvents based on their interactions with the polymer chains. Good solvents have a strong affinity for the polymer and leading to a rise in swelling. These solvents interact favorably with the polymer chains and causing the chains to unfold and absorb solvent molecules \[[39](#_bookmark58)\]. On the other hand, poor solvents exhibit weak in-teractions with the polymer and resulting in limited swelling or even shrinkage of the hydrogel. Poor solvents can induce chain collapse and aggregation or reducing the swelling capacity of the hydrogel. The polymer-solvent interaction parameter is denoted as χ (chi). It demon-strates the compatibility between the polymer and solvent. A positive χ value indicates favorable exchanges of polymer and solvent and pro-moting swelling behavior. In contrast, a negative χ value suggests un-favorable interactions and leading to reduced swelling. The magnitude of χ influences the degree of solvation, polymer chain expansion or contraction and directly impacting the swelling. Other parameters like temperature, pH, and presence of additives can also influence the swelling property and degree of hydrogels \[[40](#_bookmark59)\]. Changes in temperature can alter the solvent properties, polymer chain conformation and affecting the swelling behavior. Changes in pH can impact the swelling capacity by causing modifications to charge density and ionization states. Additionally, the incorporation of additives or functional groups can modify the polymer-solvent interactions and leading to tailored swelling behavior for specific applications. Understanding the interplay between network density, solvent type and the polymer-solvent inter-action parameter is crucial for designing hydrogels with desired swelling

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 5.** Hydrogel swelling mechanism.

properties. By carefully selecting the network density, solvent and polymer composition, researchers can manipulate the swelling behavior to achieve optimal performance \[[41](#_bookmark60)\]. Rubber elastic theory has been considered as an effective approach for elucidating the mechanical be-haviors of hydrogels. As it provides a framework that connects three critical bulk characteristics: rubbery modulus scale, crosslinking density and temperature. The application of rubber elastic theory to hydrogels is based on the observation that hydrogels exhibit elastic properties similar to those of rubber materials. However, the classic rubber theory alone is insufficient in explaining the specific behavior of hydrogels in aqueous media and necessitating modifications and adaptations. Hydrogels, un-like conventional rubber materials and exist in a swollen state when immersed in aqueous environments. The presence of water significantly influences their mechanical properties and introduces additional com-plexities that are not accounted for in the classic rubber elastic theory. Hydrogels are highly hydrated and water molecules become integral components of polymer network and influencing overall behavior of hydrogel. The interactions of these chains with water molecules and having hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions \[[42](#_bookmark61)\]. It can determine the mechanical response of hydrogels in aqueous media. To address these unique characteristics, modifications and extensions to the classic rubber elastic theory have been proposed. These modifications incorporate additional parameters to account for the swelling behavior and water-polymer interactions specific to hydrogels. One such modi-fication is the introduction of Flory-Rehner theory that considers the equilibrium swelling of hydrogels based on polymer-solvent in-teractions. The Flory-Rehner theory incorporates factors such as polymer-solvent interaction parameter, solvent quality and osmotic pressure to provide a more accurate description of hydrogel swelling. Furthermore, the classic rubber elastic theory assumes isotropy and homogeneity in the material and which may not fully capture the complex nature of hydrogels. Hydrogels often exhibit structural het-erogeneities, anisotropy and non-linear mechanical behavior. Which cannot be adequately described by the simple linear elastic model of rubber materials. Advanced mechanical models, such as non-linear elasticity theory, finite element analysis and viscoelastic models have

been employed to account for these complexities and provide a more comprehensive understanding of mechanical behavior of hydrogel \[[40](#_bookmark59)\]. Cellulose-based hydrogels, with their diverse structural configura-tions and crosslinking possibilities, exhibit a wide range of characteris-tics, making them adaptable for various applications. The biodegradability and swelling mechanisms of these hydrogels are pivotal traits that can be fine-tuned through modifications in cross-linking density, polymer composition, or functionalization. Crosslinking density plays a crucial role, as higher density enhances mechanical stability but reduces swelling, while lower density increases swelling at the cost of structural integrity. Polymer-solvent interactions, charac-terized by the polymer-solvent interaction parameter, significantly in-fluence swelling, with favorable interactions promoting expansion and unfavorable interactions limiting it. The existence of hydrophilic groups, like sodium carboxylate, enhances swelling by increasing electrostatic repulsion and osmotic pressure, leading to polymer coil expansion \[[43](#_bookmark62)\]. Environmental factors like pH, temperature, and ionic strength further affect swelling behavior, with pH and temperature-sensitive hydrogels exhibiting reversible transitions. Additives and functional groups can also be incorporated to tailor swelling properties for specific applica-tions. Advanced mechanical models, including Flory-Rehner theory and modified rubber elastic models, provide insights into the interplay of swelling, polymer-solvent interactions, and structural heterogeneities, enabling the design of hydrogels with optimal swelling and mechanical characteristics. By understanding and manipulating these factors, hydrogels based on cellulose can be engineered for enhanced adapt-ability and functionality in biomedical, environmental and industrial

applications \[[44](#_bookmark63)\].

- 1.  _Biodegradability of hydrogel based on cellulose_

The degradability of hydrogel in anaerobic/aerobic environment is a crucial property that greatly influences their potential. Numerous methods are being employed to modify the properties of naturally occurring polymers by incorporating suitable monomers for industrial usage.

The biodegradation is a crucial property that greatly influences their potential for various applications. These hydrogels undergo degradation in both anaerobic and aerobic environments is highly advantageous. As it allows for their safe and efficient disposal after use without causing environmental harm. To further enhance the biodegradability, various methods are being employed to modify the properties of naturally occurring polymers \[[45](#_bookmark64)\]. For example, cellulose is modified by intro-ducing ester groups, such as carboxymethyl or methyl groups, that in-fluences the hydrophilicity and biodegradability of the resulting hydrogels. In addition to chemical modification, physical methods can also be employed to tailor the biodegradability. The degradation de-pends on adjusting the porosity of the hydrogel network. A less dense crosslinking network or a higher porosity allows for easier penetration of enzymes and microorganisms and accelerating the degradation process. Conversely, a more densely cross-linked structure or a lower porosity can result in slower degradation. The biodegradability of cellulose-based hydrogels not only benefits tissue engineering but also extends to other areas like drug delivery and environmental applications \[[46](#_bookmark65)\]. In biodegradable hydrogels can act as carriers for controlled release and gradually releasing therapeutic agents while ultimately degrading and eliminating from the body. In environmental applications, they can be utilized for water purification, soil remediation and other eco-friendly practices where the hydrogel can degrade naturally over time and minimizing environmental pollution. The biodegradation is influenced by the composition of hydrogel, its structural characteristics, the pres-ence of enzymes or microorganisms and the surrounding environmental conditions. The rate and extent of degradation can be tailored to meet specific application requirements through careful design and optimiza-tion of hydrogel formulation \[[46](#_bookmark65)\]. Feng et al., performed a research where they synthesized a superabsorbent polymer using cellulose

derived from flax shive, _N_, _N_′-methylenebisacrylamide and potassium

persulfate \[[47](#_bookmark66)\]. The resulting sample exhibited decent biodegradability

through soil composting. Over a period of 54 days at 40 ◦C, the super-absorbent polymer underwent biological degradation of up to 40 %. In another research effort, a novel double degradable hydrogel made up of

yeast, carboxymethyl cellulose and polyvinyl alcohol was developed \[[48](#_bookmark67)\]. The yeast as a foaming agent enhanced the biodegradability and significantly enhanced polyvinyl alcohol degradation within hydrogel. Maximum degradation observed was 45 ± 2.8 %. As a result of their

biocompatibility and biodegradability they hold promising material for

various industrial and medical usages \[[49](#_bookmark68)\].

# Synthesis techniques for cellulose based hydrogels

The polymerization process determines the applications and quali-ties of the finalized polymer. In general, step-growth polymerization and chain-growth processes are utilized for polymer synthesis. In former, there are covalent bonds among the monomer’s functional groups. The solution and melt polycondensation are two methods used in step-growth polymerization. In polymerization by chain-growth, the mono-mers are activated to form a longer polymer chain \[[50](#_bookmark69)\]. Free radicals are typically produced by an initiator utilizing energy sources like light and heat to activate. These free radicals further activate the monomeric chain and form the free radicals on the monomer. The polymer chain grows concurrently with the surrounding monomers being activated by the active monomers. This polymerization process uses a variety of ap-proaches, including emulsion, bulk, solution, and suspension polymer-ization \[[51](#_bookmark70)\].

The polymer chains in hydrogels join through crosslinks to form a network with three dimensions. The physical characteristics of polymer chains are affected by cross-linking, which includes elasticity, tough-ness, strength, solubility and melting point, to mention a few. Because cross-links restrict the rate of rotation between the polymer chains and glass transition temperature of cross-linked polymers is higher. In a hydrogel, cross-linking might be chemical or physical \[[52](#_bookmark71)\].

- 1.  _Chemical crosslinking_

In the case of hydrogel polymerization, chemical cross-linkages include chain growth, gamma, electron beam, addition, and condensa-tion polymerization. This kind of polymerization uses initiation, prop-agation and termination steps along with cationic, anionic, and free radical. Monomer units are joined to the active sites produced by free radicals during the initiation stage of the chain-growth polymerization process and which results in the production of the hydrogel \[[53](#_bookmark72)\].

Additions to the polymerization by free radical, chemically cross-linked hydrogels are also produced using Schiff base cross-linking pro-cesses and click chemistry. Click reactions are often quick, flexible, efficient, regio-specific and produce no byproducts. Azide-alkyne cy-cloadditions, thiol-ene reactions, Diels-Alder reactions and oxide re-actions are the click reaction types that can produce hydrogels. The polymers should have amine, hydrazide or alcohol functionalities for Schiff base cross-linking. The network of molecules is formed through the reaction of these functional groups with aldehydes \[[54](#_bookmark73)\].

Chemical crosslinking often emphasizes on the connections that connect crosslinking agent and polymer. Hydrogel’s characteristics, mainly its mechanical strength is caused by a particular functional group of crosslinking agent. Glutaraldehyde may crosslink hydroxyl group-containing polymers under adverse conditions, such as high tempera-tures, low pH levels, and the use of methanol as a quencher. Hydrogels can be developed through crosslinking polysaccharides with divinyl sulfone, 1, 6-hexamethylene diisocyanate, and several other chemicals \[[55](#_bookmark74)\]. These chemicals are used to make sure that a certain polymer or functional group forms a network of linkages in order to prepare hydrogels.

- 1.  _Physical crosslinking_

The cross-links observed in physically cross-linked hydrogels are caused by physical processes like crystallization, self-assembly, and hydrogen bonding. The molecules with O H, N H or F H functionality form hydrogen bonds with one other. When low molecular solutes or bulk solvents crystallize after freezing and polymer chain space is reduced. The concentration of polymer is increased and polymer chain is forced to align and associate within the connecting network structure of a hydrogel. This process is known as the freeze-thaw method \[[56](#_bookmark75)\]. Typically, covalent interactions and hydrogen bonds hold the linked network formed through this approach.

Ultra-visible light is one type of high-energy irradiation that triggers the photo crosslinking or photo initiator process. This has drawn sig-nificant notice due to how quickly in-situ gelation happens. This process is known as the radiation-induced crosslinking technique. The process of creating hydrogels via radiation-induced crosslinking is harmless to the environment \[[57](#_bookmark76)\]. This method’s benefits include the ability to syn-thesize homogeneous hydrogel quickly and efficiently in a single step without the need for a catalyst or chemicals. As well as the ability to regulate the process by adjusting the radiation and dosage rate.

The synthesis techniques for cellulose-based hydrogels play a crucial role in determining their structural, mechanical, and functional prop-erties. Both physical and chemical crosslinking methods are integral to the formation of stable three-dimensional polymer networks. Chemical crosslinking, with its reliance on covalent bonds and various polymeri-zation mechanisms like chain growth, click reactions and Schiff base processes, provides enhanced mechanical strength and durability to the hydrogels. Meanwhile, physical crosslinking, which leverages non-covalent interactions like hydrogen bonding, self-assembly and crys-tallization, offers eco-friendly and versatile approaches for hydrogel synthesis.

Each crosslinking method presents distinct advantages and limita-tions, making the choice of technique application-specific. Chemical crosslinking ensures robust and enduring networks, often suitable for demanding applications, while physical crosslinking methods enable

environmentally sustainable and rapid synthesis with minimal chemical additives. Thus, a thorough comprehension of these crosslinking pro-cesses is necessary for tailoring cellulose-based hydrogels to meet diverse industrial and environmental needs.

# Mechanism of adsorption

Adsorption has emerged as an efficient approach for removing inorganic and organic pollutants like dyes and heavy metals. When it comes to adsorption there are numerous types of materials being used, mainly consisting of activated carbon adsorbent, bio adsorbent, nano adsorbent, hydrogels, etc. Among these adsorbents, hydrogel offers va-riety of benefits over the other materials. Hydrogels have high water retention capabilities; this allows them to capture more of the pollutants from the solution. Some hydrogels, such as cellulose-based hydrogels are biocompatible and environmentally friendly, aligning well with sus-tainable practices. Additionally, they are more cost-effective to produce compared to other materials, making them highly suitable for large-scale operations. The adsorption on the hydrogel material is accom-plished by several different mechanism, including, reduction, ion ex-change, and electrostatic interaction \[[58](#_bookmark77)\].

The reduction adsorption shows chemisorption nature, i.e., involving chemical reaction. The metal ions get attracted through oppositely charged surface of the adsorbent, which results in metal cation re-ductions. This process results in precipitation of cations over the adsorbent surface. Wang et al. (2022) studied the effect of hydrogel coating on adsorption capabilities of montmorillonite for removing Cr

(VI). The coating of cellulose over the material was confirmed through the presence of peak at 22◦. FTIR analysis of prepared samples suggested synergetic impact of synthesis processes causing formation of desired

material. Maximum removal efficiency of 98.08 % was achieved. The mechanism followed by the adsorption was also analysed. It was concluded that the elimination of Cr(VI) was because of direct reduction of Cr(VI) and Fe(II). The hydrogel coating offers a shell for nanosized material and act as transport channel for introducing the Cr(VI) to active sites of material. This is possible due to the porous three-dimensional structure of hydrogel. The study showed that introduction of cellulose based hydrogel provided higher degradation efficiencies for elimination of Cr(VI) by reducing it to Cr(III) and produced Cr(III) gets adsorbed between layers of prepared material. This reduces the overall toxicity of the treated system \[[59](#_bookmark78)\].

In ion exchange process, there is an exchange in ions between adsorbate and adsorbent. This mechanism is highly dependent on pH of reaction media, because of presence of excess ions. There are some works which shows that, cellulose based hydrogels, follows the ion ex-change process for adsorption. Zhou et al. (2012) examined the adsorption of the heavy metal cations (i.e., Ni(II), Cd(II), and Pb(II)) over the cellulose hydrogel. They prepared cellulose-graft-acrylic acid hydrogel using the phosphoric acid. The samples prepared were found to have followed ion exchange among metal cations and nonionic or ionic groups contained in the hydrogel. The suggested adsorption mechanisms for the prepared samples were confirmed through FTIR analysis. The analysis explained that the FTIR spectra varied significantly before adsorption and after adsorption. The weak stretching peak of -COOH at

1726 cm—1 was shifted to lower wave number of 1712 cm—1, 1716 cm—1 and 1718 cm—1. The shift also became sharper with the adsorption. The peak observed for absorption band at 1598 cm—1 were for the stretching of -C=O in carboxylate which was also shifted to lower angles with different adoption. This study indicates that -COO— group could be the

primary active site for the adsorption process. The highest removal tendency of 825.7 mg/g was reached for Pb(II), followed by Cd(II) showing 562.7 mg/g of adsorption and Ni(II) showing 380.1 mg/g of adsorption. The reusability analysis explained that the samples can be reused up to three times with a loss of 15 % of adsorption capacities \[[60](#_bookmark79)\].

The electrostatic adsorption occurs when the adsorbent and

adsorbate are oppositely charged and there exist an electrostatic inter-action among both of them. This type of adsorption is pH sensitive. This interaction is governed by the Zeta potential, which indicates the dif-ference in potential of particle and its surrounding medium. Zeta po-tential determines the magnitude of the interaction. The zeta potential is impacted by the pH, at the pH where Zeta potential reaches zero is termed as pH of zero charge. At zero charge there is no net electrostatic interaction between adsorbate and adsorbent. Inversely, at extreme pH the interaction within the adsorbent and adsorbate is governed via the electrostatic interaction. Peng et al. examined the adsorption behavior of the cellulose-clay hydrogels. The pollutant utilized for adsorption was the methylene blue. The samples showed MB removal efficiencies of 98

% for a solution having MB concentration 100 mg/L. The study specu-lated that the main driving force for the adsorption process was the electrostatic and hydrophobic interaction \[[61](#_bookmark80)\].

Tie et al., prepared a bio-based hydrogel (cellulose nanocrystals/ alginate-Fe(II)) made from cellulose nanocrystals/alginate induced by ferrous ions for the adsorption of tetracycline \[[62](#_bookmark81)\]. The adsorption mechanism of Tetracycline onto the cellulose nanocrystals/alginate-Fe (_II_)hydrogel is explained through a combination of several key in-teractions shown in the [Fig. 6](#_bookmark15). The cellulose nanocrystals/alginate-Fe(_II_) hydrogel has a special open-framework structure with uniform channels that allow TC molecules to easily reach the pores, where they are trap-ped inside. The process mainly works through surface complexation, where electrons from tetracycline oxygen and nitrogen groups bond with Fe(II) ions, forming stable Fe-O/N-tetracycline complexes. This complexation is stronger than that with Fe(III) or Ca(II) due to tetra-cycline varied binding sites.

Other mechanisms also play a role, including cation bridging, where the metal ions help connect the tetracycline molecules to the hydrogel. Additionally, n-π EDA (electron donor-acceptor) interactions, hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions all contribute to tetracycline adsorption. Functional groups in tetracycline, like phenol, hydroxyl, and amino groups, form these interactions with the hydrogel’s surface. At certain pH levels, the tetracycline molecules are attracted to the hydrogel through electrostatic forces due to the hydrogel’s negative charge.

In conclusion, the combination of electrostatic interactions, cation bridging, and hydrogen bonds is essential for efficient removal of tetracycline from wastewater. These interactions enable the cellulose nanocrystals/alginate-Fe(_II_)hydrogel to effectively adsorb and retain tetracycline, making it a promising solution for treating pharmaceutical and hospital wastewater. Furthermore, improvements in the hydrogel’s design, such as incorporating antimicrobial agents and optimizing its pore structure, could enhance its recyclability and long-term use in real-world applications.
